text_fidelity_a:
Belkin 8-Outlet AV Power Strip Surge Protector with 6-Foot Power Cord and 2 USB Charging Ports, 3000 Joules, Black (BV108050-06-BLK) I love that this surge protector and plug strip has two USB ports for charging my Kindle and cell phone, but the placement of the USB ports, which is a major selling point for this unit, is hindered by the position of the cord wrap feature as well as the areas to plug in your larger electronics that have the big boxy plug. The USB ports are tucked right in between the cord wrap spot and the place to plug in larger plugs, so if one isn't blocking your USB ports, the other is.

In addition, I kind of wish that the majority of the plugs were spaced farther apart. I have a few electronics that have very small boxy plugs, and those don't fit right next to one another on the main area of the plug strip. The only thing that will fit on those plugs without overlapping are the traditional small plugs that are on lamps and other uncomplicated items. I don't have too many of those, and I'm guessing that most people buy plug strips because they have a bunch of electronics, almost all of which would have those bigger boxy plugs.

That said, the surge protector feature is absolutely effective, and I know this because we had PG&E replacing some poles in our neighborhood recently and we had many incidences of brownouts, surges, and spotty power, and this unit kept any harm from coming to any of my electronics that were plugged into it.

And while it is easy to make design suggestions, I have to say that I haven't found the perfect plug strip yet. Almost all of them seem to have some design characteristics that make them not quite ideal. While this unit is not perfectly designed with regards to the placement of the USB ports and the spacing of the regular plugs, it is certainly a high-quality, very functional unit that does what it says it does, and I trust the Belkin brand that it's going to function for some time. This plug strip is also nice in that it has a space so that you can mount it on the wall or on the back of your desk if you so desire.
text_fidelity_b: Belkin 8-Outlet AV Power Strip Surge Protector with 6-Foot Power Cord and 2 USB Charging Ports, 3000 Joules, Black (BV108050-06-BLK)

text_fidelity_a:
Legrand - Wiremold Cable Management Kit, Cord Organizer and Hider, Concealer, C210S Cord Cover Kit, White I'm sure they do it for shipping purposes and to appeal to homeowners without tools, but I don't like that they give you multiple short pieces instead of fewer long pieces that you could cut down to appropriate size. That just means you need more couplers; each additional coupler decreases the appeal of the final installation.

Honestly, I hate surface mounted conduit. But there are times when it is required, and in those cases better than nothing. I own my home, so of course I put all permanent links properly inside the walls, but even then, there are times when the Cat/RG/other jacks are not directly behind the furniture holding the devices that need the cables. In these cases, I prefer to mount these with screws, and then caulk and paint them into the painted baseboards so they blend in better, although they have made these with tape for truly temporary installations.

There is just one connector for an inside corner and an outside corner (on the x/z axis). And in my opinion, these are the only two you should really need, and you probably need more of them. I am never going vertical up walls with cables; I just go from the jack along the baseboard to behind the furniture...if I need more than that, I'm afraid I need to just stop being lazy and tear down a wall or something.

I get that if you are in an apartment or a rental property, you may need more flexibility with this. But in my opinion, if you can't do a proper wall-mount TV install without surface-mount conduit, then you should just use a TV stand as God intended because this is not enough to make cables acceptable in such an install (although honestly, it is better than nothing).
text_fidelity_b: Legrand - Wiremold Cable Management Kit, Cord Organizer and Hider, Concealer, C210S Cord Cover Kit, White

Amazon Basics Adjustable Tablet/iPad Mount Holder for Microphone and Music Stand, Black So when I ordered this mount, it was based on the title description and one small photo. Here's what I've learned since.

It's meant to be mounted to a post like what might be a part of a monitor stand. So the clamp is the shape of a hook. It does not clamp well onto flat surfaces. I wanted to mount this onto a shelf board, so I've got a plastic tube inserted on the hook side to occupy space to help it sit flat.

The holders are not spring loaded. Each end is tighten by a knob. The knobs can be difficult to access depending on the orientation of the arm. In my case one of the knob was right up against the arm. So you don't just walk up and slide you tablet into this, it needs to be set up.

The rounded retainers are plastic, not rubber. So you can't just have them on both sides. The have to be on the top or bottom or in opposing corners.

As a tablet it holder, it works. But there are far more user friendly designs out there.

I hope you found this review a little bit helpful. Thank you for reading.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Adjustable Tablet/iPad Mount Holder for Microphone and Music Stand, Black

RayHom 8 Bay AA AAA Battery Charger, Double Charging Speed with LCD Display Independent Slot for Ni-MH AA AAA Rechargeable Batteries This is a nice alternative to chargers that require you to charge batteries in pairs. There are spaces for eight batteries, and you can charge any number within them, and mix and match AA and AAA. The eight spaces are divided electrically into two banks of four spaces, and the manufacturer says each bank can provide 2000 mA of charging power (which lowers as you add more batteries and the current is divided between them). However, the included adapter only provides only 1200 mA (so says its label), so I'm not sure the math checks out.

I gave it a test with an assortment of different brand and capacity rechargeables, then checked the batteries with a multimeter. Even fully loaded the charger worked pretty quickly and brought each one up to just over 1.4 volts. I have a brand-name charger that will bring them up to 1.5 volts, but that may be overcharging a bit and might reduce overall battery life.

The one minor negative is that the battery icons on the backlit display are pretty much invisible unless you bend down or tilt the charger up to see them. You can see how low the angle is in the photo I uploaded.

Other than that, convenient and reasonably fast, it's a nice charger.
text_fidelity_b: RayHom 8 Bay AA AAA Battery Charger, Double Charging Speed with LCD Display Independent Slot for Ni-MH AA AAA Rechargeable Batteries

Unfortunately, functionality wise, the bag is just okay. Maybe a little below average.

The bag is also stiff. If I had a laptop and over-ear headphones in it at the same time, I couldn’t get the flap to buckle, even after adjusting the straps. The bag doesn’t handle bulk very well.

Unfortunately, I’ll have to go back to using a regular backpack instead of this much cooler looking leather messenger bag.

Canon PowerShot A1400 16.0 MP Digital Camera with 5x Digital Image Stabilized Zoom 28mm Wide-Angle Lens and 720p HD Video Recording (Black) (OLD MODEL) These cameras are amazing. Get a 32GB chip, put CHDK on it and you can do awesome stuff with this camera. I bought two for my family's trip to Alaska, and we snapped thousands of photos. Very good quality, fair low light performance, controls are easy enough. We spent a fair bit of time learning the controls so we'd be fluent with them.

Here's a neat trick: You can use these cameras as low power microscopes. Put the Macro setting on, take a photo as near ask the thing will focus, which is pretty close, then hit 'Play' and use the zoom lever on the shutter release to zoom in and get a microscope view of what you took the photo of.

Also, with CHDK on the SD card, you have a built in intervelometer for taking time lapse sequences.

Another fun thing to do is to take night time photos of the sky using the long exposure setting. With the 10 second setting and the ISO turned up you can capture images of stars or northern lights in the night sky. Fantastic for a $60 camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon PowerShot A1400 16.0 MP Digital Camera with 5x Digital Image Stabilized Zoom 28mm Wide-Angle Lens and 720p HD Video Recording (Black) (OLD MODEL)

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Technology Speaker - Wireless - Bluetooth - USB, Bluetooth Let's do the pro/con thing.

Pros:

+ Sound is definitely amazing coming from 1 amp @ 5 volts. I wouldn't have guessed that was quite possible. And the stereo effect works well, especially if you're positioned indirectly to the speaker (i.e., not right beside it). That said, it's not an amazing amount better than the SBX8, so I wonder if the (untested by me) SBX10 would be the sweet spot in terms of size to sound ratio.

+ Integrated microphone features work well, although I'm still not sold on voice commands.

+ Bluetooth combined with direct AC power option makes it truly versatile.

+ This would be awesome to have as the communications centerpiece in a temporary apartment while on the road, to use in any room that doesn't have speakers, or even as a centerpiece in a smaller apartment. That said, it's a bit large to want to travel on planes with, but I would do it for a long trip.

+ As long as you're getting your power via an electrical outlet (and NOT a computer, although as an "ejected" (from the computer) device, it should work as well), you are able to communicate to the speaker with bluetooth and with the line in jack, which allows this to be a more permanent fixture. You can have it work with your phone and still be hooked up to a more permanent sound source. In fact, the speaker will play two sources at once in that case, but a full USB connection to a computer shuts it off to the rest of the world (i.e., in that case, it will ignore the line in and the bluetooth connections.

+ Cool capacitive touch controls.

Cons:

- No way to shut it off short of unplugging. This makes a more permanent setup less attractive. Not that it's eating much power just sitting there, but still...

- Included (thankfully) AC adapter could be smaller and shaped more efficiently. It comes with plugs for US, Continental Europe, UK, and Australia (which covers most of the world since most countries use one of those), but the latter two hang off the front of the unit awkwardly. You couldn't plug it in beside most AC adapters. Anyway, most people have some other ones sitting around if this one is not adequate.

- My BB - although it recognizes the device as a SoundBlaster SBX20, not generically - cannot control the volume like a bluetooth headset I use. This must be done from the integrated controls.

- I have to reinitiate bluetooth connection from my phone (thankfully not from the unit) after each power down. Actually not sure if this is a pro or a con...depends on your thinking.

In summary, this is a really cool, versatile device with a lot of interesting features. It is a niche, however. I'd call it just about perfect for someone on a long term assignment away from home and perfect for some people as an in-house permanent setup, although the lack of a power switch bothers me for those uses. It's a bit large for short term travel unless by personal vehicle. Hopefully this helps you decide if this is right for you.
text_fidelity_b: Creative Technology Speaker - Wireless - Bluetooth - USB, Bluetooth

The user's guide clearly walked me through the process even though these were the first in-wall speakers I've installed. It also comes with a very handy template to ensure it's a "cut once" process with no regrets (or spackle). Since there's a lip on the frame you don't need to be worried about making a perfectly smooth cut through the drywall since the rough edges are hidden.

I was torn between these and the RC80i model. Both had identical tech specs on the Polk site. What sealed the deal in terms of the RC85i model is that it is a bit more shallow than the RC80i (depth of 2 and 7/8 inches for the RC85i versus 3 and 1/4 inches with the RC80i). More importantly, the tweeter assembly on the RC85i is a bit different. According to Polk, the tweeter in the 85i has a plate underneath it that helps project the sound. This is not found in the 80i.

But the proof is in the sound, and these sound wonderful. I'm using them in a basement wired to a Denon AV receiver in the LR. While the sound can't compete with the Kef's I have in the LR, the Polks sound far better than I expected given the price. Very pleased!

They also are very aesthetically pleasing. The grill is nicely made, and can be painted. As with installation, clear and detailed instructions on painting the grills are in the user's guide.

Good sound, good looks and good price - can't ask for more! Highly recommend.

Dzees 5W Solar Panel for Wireless Outdoor Security Camera, Compatible with Rechargeable Battery Powered Camera, Continuous Solar Power for Camera, Waterproof, Reliable and Non-Stop Green Charging This is the fourth camera from this company that I purchased and I have to say that I find the value to be overall a good deal. The main problem that I fine with them is when mounted outdoors they tend to fail after 2 to 3 months sometimes in other cases they last as long as a year but in every case they end up failing.

The really frustrating thing is that once they die there’s no way to bring them back and the battery life just doesn’t seem to last past a few months of outdoor abuse.

When paired with a solar charger they actually do quite well and are not problem to keep outside for Several weeks without charging.

The main drawback to this type of system is that it only records when there’s motion this is in order to save battery life and it has a small chip that does motion to Engage the camera once there’s actually motion going on.

Because of this many people are surprised that they can’t look at a point in time and see what was going on they have to only look at the motion events that are raised by the camera. All in all for a cheap and quick solution these were great if you need to monitor something critical I would look for another resource.
text_fidelity_b: Dzees 5W Solar Panel for Wireless Outdoor Security Camera, Compatible with Rechargeable Battery Powered Camera, Continuous Solar Power for Camera, Waterproof, Reliable and Non-Stop Green Charging

text_fidelity_a:
Fire Kids Edition Tablet, 7" Display, 8 GB, Blue Kid-Proof Case (Previous Generation - 5th) Very disappointed in Amazon. They ALMOST Got it right. Returned this one quickly.

Let me be clear I am an Amazon Fangirl. I have consistently tried their new things, I have subscribed to prime for years, I love amazon. I love their kindles. So I don't often speak ill of my precious amazon.

I wanted to upgrade my son's kindle ( First gen Fire HD7 ) it's charging port is a bit wobbly and damaged, we've used it for many years and it's got a little wear. That said, it works BETTER Than the current kindle fire. The only problem is you can't play all the same games that I can play on my other kindle and you can't on the new one either. It wants the "NEW HD" ( or my HDX) to play certain games.

Where to begin....first of all the new OS Sucks. It just does. so bad. I'm not even going to rant on that because it's user preference but I found the old OS to be more user friendly and responsive. I have an HDX and it's by far the top notch of them all. I hope I don't have to "upgrade" to this OS.

Storage & Offline use:
You only have 8gb of storage, which wouldn't be an issue thanks to the upgradable microsd slot.. ( GOOD CALL AMAZON) ..EXCEPT They crippled the functionality. For example, I go to the grocery store or road tip with my kid and I let him watch or play on his kindle without being on wifi, you can't do that anymore. Your kids can NOT Watch movies that are downloaded to the microsd card when you are offline. You can't. Not allowed. You can't operate much of anything in the kids profile if you are not connected to wifi. Having 128bg SD card is USELESS for your kids when offline.
I've bought loads of disney movies and the digital copies are all on Amazon for the very reason that they were great to download to our other kindles and watch when we were in the car, plane, or costco.

It won't even let you START The kids freetime profile if you are offline. This severely cripples the device for no good reason. Games and movies which are downloaded to the device or the SD card should work offline in most cases. I've done it on my HDX and my first gen hd. Works just fine in freetime on older devices. No reason for this. And before someone tells me that's what you expect when you stream...I'm not talking about streaming or using netflix, I'm talking about content downloaded to the device. Irrationally Amazon decided that if you are not online, you can go kick rocks.
If you are in an ADULT Profile, I think you can, although I did not try to be fair, because I bought the KIDS Edition for a reason, for my kid to use it.I have my own kindle. No sense in having this for kids if you can't use it when you're out and about. Everyone knows that the screen is the ultimate "quiet time" reward in our parent tool-kit. If you say it's not you're either a liar or an over taxed helicopter parent with way too much techno anxiety. Joking...sorry not sorry.

Kindle FreeTime "unlimited"....
I use the freetime for my son ALL THE TIME. It's amazing, it limits him to what *I* want him to play and watch. I can set a timer for weekends/weekdays that go off at bedtime so that he can "read", watch a show, or play for a short time as a reward before bed. The freetime is
the number one reason I have not gone with an iPad or other device. I can't give my kid any other device with the same level of comfort and control of his screen time and content. I HIGHLY recommend kindles to all my parent friends for this exact reason. It's WELL Worth it. However...it's NOT worth it to use "Unlimited" on this new device. The new kindle sucks for freetime ( See above reason on offline freetime) Mainly tho...it's TERRIBLE for the parent if you've mistakenly turned ON Kindle unlimited. ( If you have an older child, say 9yrs+ this can be mitigated with a nice sit down convo) I'll explain...

Why Freetime Unlimited SUCKS:
I'm speaking of the paid Unlimited service here, the main feature of freetime is still great, with some exceptions ( above) on the new device.

Every single app they touch it will download. If they are curious, and want to see what the game is they instinctively click the app, completely unaware that they have 8gb of space on their tablet and actually it's more like 4gb after the OS. This makes it run Slooooooow and crash. Crash a lot. Crash within the first 60 minutes of your child using the device. Until you go in and fix it, meaning delete them all individually, this device is annoyingly slow and unresponsive. I found out, you can get the apps to download or move them to the memory card, but it will still slow you down once that fills up and you still have to do regular maintaince on the devices memory. The first year of this is free, with this device, but I promise you it's more annoying than worth it. I was an early unlimited subscriber at $2.99 a month and I cancelled it rather quickly, even on my far better HDX and the first gen kindle it was STILL Annoying.

If you have an OLDER Child...this may be mitigated with a sit down conversation as to how their device works, what downloading means, and their storage space. My child is 5, and has proven to not exactly get the concept and download everything willy nilly if given the option.

Do yourself a favor....buy the HD Version, Pray they didn't cripple offline freetime on it, buy the extra warranty and case and and try that instead. That's what I plan to do, I'm going to give it a wait and see if they improve the HD device on the next round. Since the first gen HD 7 still works better than this one, I'll hold out.

Please Amazon....try to get it right next time.
Thanks,
Just another mom.
text_fidelity_b: Fire Kids Edition Tablet, 7" Display, 8 GB, Blue Kid-Proof Case (Previous Generation - 5th)

text_fidelity_a: Meade 505 Telescope to PC Cable CP2102 USB RS232 to 4P4C RJ10 Adapter Control Console Cable for Mead 505 Telescope (6FT, for Meade) Worked fine once I realized the cable is a UART and I had to install a driver for it. Looked it up on the web and found one, but it wouldn’t auto-install. I had to manually install it. Suddenly, COM4 appeared and there was the mount. My mount is an LX200GPS, and I still need to connect the handset for this to work, sadly. text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell 3 – enhanced wifi, improved motion detection, easy installation Great wireless camera/doorbell. Hardware/software this is ideal. We live on a busy street so we were getting lots of notifications. The software allowed us to adjust where the camera sensed motion, cutting down "false" notifications. Easy to use.
Easy to setup and install. Took maybe 15 minutes from opening the box to having it up and running.
Convenient set-up and access via phone (iOS and Android) app. Added skill to Echo, so when someone sets of camera or pushes doorbell, we get a notification via Alexa, and an image on the Echo show. You can adjust how often and what notifications you receive in the app.
Night vision is pretty good as well. Another nice feature is you can access a "live" view anytime, notification or not.
Audio works well, so if you are in the basement, garage, at work, shopping you can talk to whomever is at your door.
If you carry your phone everywhere or have a smart home speaker (Google, Echo or maybe Apple?) you won't need the additional chime, phone and speakers have a decently loud sound.
I would suggest getting a second battery if you have a busy street or lots of activity. The app notifies you in plenty of time the battery is low and needs to be recharged (only takes a couple hours to fully charge). But a second battery extends the life and less work (but to be fair, one screw using included driver, slide off plate, slide battery out, set to charge and reverse process to put battery back in. With two batteries, the whole thing takes about two minutes. With one, you simply have a non-functioning doorbell/camera for a few hours. No biggie, just FYI.
Also there is an an App called Neighbors free to join and use. It lets you share "videos and notifications of criminal or suspicious activity. So if someone in your neighborhood is broken into or home is vandalized they can share the video and/or share a notice of the incident. Lost dog, share. Delivery thieves, share. So both kinda cool and scary.
Now the BAD. To access the video you have to pay a monthly fee ( now if you access the video within the first 30 seconds or so, you are golden, but if you have your hands full, or can't access your phone, you can't see the video, or back it up. While the basic few is like $40 ish a year. Higher for the next tier up. That is forever. And no easy way to back up to a local storage device. All files are on Rings servers.
Now if you know that up front, and $40 is no biggie. Then 5 stars.
But for me that is an issue.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell 3 – enhanced wifi, improved motion detection, easy installation

text_fidelity_a:
Canon EOS 5D Mark II 21.1MP Full Frame CMOS Digital SLR Camera with EF 24-105mm f/4 L IS USM Lens (OLD MODEL) I've used and throughly enjoyed a 5D for a couple of years, and have found it to be a simply outstanding full-frame camera. Like a lot of people, I was eagerly looking forward to the 5D Mark II, and pre-ordered one. After using it for a few weeks, I am pleased to report that this is an excellent update to the 5D.

If you're researching this camera, you've probably heard about the "black dot" problem (basically, some dark pixels to the right of blown highlights). Unless you're printing photos in the several feet by several feet size, you'll never see them. Sure, I'll download a firmware fix when it's available, but in the meantime, I've never encountered even the slightest problem in real-world use.

Size and controls are very comparable to the 5D - you'll feel at ease very quickly. The viewfinder is fantastic -- bigger, brighter, and a very welcome addition. There are many "under the skin" upgrades, the biggest being 21.1 megapixels. So much more flexibility in shooting, but be prepared for some huge raw files! A processor upgrade (DIGIC 4) keeps things moving along at a good clip. I can't comment on the HD video capture since I'm just dabbling with it at the moment and have essentially no experience as a videographer. But, looking forward to learning. The video capture was just icing on the cake for me - bought it for still photos.

Disappointments are very few and far between, such as the fact that the battery pack is a different design, so it can't be interchanged with the 5D. Supposedly, it has a longer life, but model interchangeability would be nice to keep the add-on costs down. I also regularly shoot with my 40D and Rebel (with the latter converted to IR), so the greater the interchangeability, the better.

In short, this is an outstanding camera, and one that will be a welcome addition to anyone's kit. If you already have a 5D and use it a lot, the Mark II is well worth the cost. The kit is a good value versus the body -- the 24-105 f/4 L IS is one of the best walk around lens available. Should you not have a need for it, you can get a good price for it on the used market.

If you're presently working with a crop sensor camera, you will be amazed at what a full frame will do for you (although, be prepared to spend some coin on some good glass -- once you get the L lens fever, you'll never want to go back!). Keep in mind that the original 5D is still available, and going at a very nice price new (and some outright steals for used bodies). The original is still a fantastic camera, and well worth considering if budget is tight.

One final point -- the RAW files are not compatable with CS3. But, the recent update to Lightroom (2.2) solves that problem. No need to update to CS4 just for that.
text_fidelity_b: Canon EOS 5D Mark II 21.1MP Full Frame CMOS Digital SLR Camera with EF 24-105mm f/4 L IS USM Lens (OLD MODEL)

text_fidelity_a:
Canon PowerShot SX280 12.1MP Digital Camera with 20x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom with 3-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL) Some people have had battery problems with this camera. I bought 2 extra Vivitar batteries with higher mA-h ratings than the stock Canon batteries. If you do the math, this camera can put a huge load on the microprocessor when you ask it to take high-rate, high-resolution videos, or multiple shots. Zoom a lot at the same time, and these little batteries aren't going to hack it. In addition, Canon has something wrong (I suspect) with the battery life sensor/indicator. (My guess is the 1.0.2.0 firmware update that's available from Canon is to help that.) On the good side, that's depressed the price of this camera. Since I don't intend to take a lot of videos with this camera, I'm OK with that. :)

I may have also gotten a good one. Over 2 days of playing with it, I've yet to change the battery. It's showing 2/3 charge. It has however, flashed "charge the battery" warnings a
couple of times.

For calibration, this is replacing a Canon A1100IS we bought about 4 years ago as a second camera.

Pro (for me):
Really good, clear pictures
Good image stabilization (hand-holding at 1/15th of a second or slower!)
Low noise, as low as ISO 1600
Large zoom range
Manual focus
DIGIC 6 processor (latest generation)
Very nice screen
P, Av, Tv & M exposure modes
Canon's basically good control layout
Small and light; carrying around a DSLR can be wearying
Wi-Fi is handy
Fits in the same case as my A1100, which was originally bought for a tiny 35 mm Vivitar I carried as a 2nd camera for years. It's marked "Samsonite World Sport, Model #20" if that helps.

Cons:
Not as good a macro capability as the A1100 (which is sterling at that one thing. I'll be keeping it for that.)
No viewfinder (unlike the A1100. It's not needed all the time, but it is handy)
Slow GPS lock in (my Nexus shows 18 or so satellites in view, and took maybe 30 sec. to lock in. The camera took several times that)
GPS power hog. (It appears to suck up a lot of power, turning it on and off a few times did seem to affect battery charge indication)
No auto bracket (To be fair, that's not common on cameras, but it should be. Canon puts it on the similar S110.)
No hyperfocal distance setting (You can do it manually, of course, but, Canon, why not add another click on the focus bar? There's a computer in there, you know)
Lithium batteries (I prefer the A1100's NiMH AAs so you can get a new set at any Staples for cheap or use alkaline AAs in a pinch)

So, with all of 2 days of experience under my belt:
1) Nice easily-portable camera at a low-ish price
2) Power hog, due to inefficient GPS, big zoom, and powerful microprocessor being pushed by video, etc.
I'll update this review someday when I have some durability information.

Update: 4/27/2014 Took a nice long walk, shot 6 min. of 720p x 30fps video and took 101 L-superfine .jpg (4k x 3k pixel) photos. This used up most of a fully-charged Vivitar 1700 mA-h battery. I got a battery warn and shutdown after my walk while reviewing the video at home. The 1000 mA-h stock Canon battery would give proportionately less life. Canon says that the stock battery is good for 210 photos. A 1700 mA-h Vivitar battery should be good for 147 more than that, or 357 photos. That means that 6 min. of 720p video is worth 256 photos! I don't think anyone will be shooting at 1080p x 60fps much.

Another way to look at it is the number of pixels processed per second by any of the 11 modes of the camera. The normal L .jpg picture takes 12.0E+6 pixels/sec (12 megapixels/sec). The least hungry mode S, takes only 0.307E+6 pixels per second. The hungriest mode is the 14 frames per second L multiple shot mode, which takes 168.E+6 pixels/sec. Since this is only in use for a few frames, it's not bad on battery life. The second worst mode 1080p x 60fps takes 124.E+6 pixels per second, 1037% of the normal L photo processing power! The 720p x 30fps mode I used is only 230% of the normal L mode. Remember, though, the single shot modes are on now and then, maybe a second out of every minute at most. The video modes are on continuously.

NB: Good cameras with a lot of features have historically eaten batteries. I carry around a handful for the A1100.

Misc.: I'm sorry to see the little A1100 get superseded; it was a trouper. Its biggest problem was auto-focusing at long zoom, which isn't a problem if you're taking snapshots in your yard, but it can be a problem if you see a magnificent vista before you. The SX280 shouldn't have a problem with that (manual zoom). YMMV

Update 7/13/2014: My one significant complaint with the SX280 was the macro focusing. As I've gotten more experience with it, some of that has gone away. The SX280's autofocus seems to work differently from the A1100's. I tend to use the macro setting less, and let the normal mode carry the freight, except in extreme cases. In many cases, that's plenty good enough. It's still not as good as the A1100, though. In all other ways, this is an amazing still camera. It also still has too small a battery. Canon seems to be phasing this one out. If you need a still camera and can find one of these cheap, you might consider it.
August, 2017 Update: 3 & a bit years after purchase, the camera is becoming unreliable, throwing E32 (lens) errors more & more frequently. That's not a bad lifespan for a point & shoot, especially with a wide-range zoom lens. The error appears to be focus related.
Sept. 2018 Update: I replaced this with a 720. Much better. I actually cured the lens error with some strong blasts into the lens gaps from canned air. That's risky, blowing dust into the camera, but in this case, it worked. The 280 is now my office camera.
text_fidelity_b: Canon PowerShot SX280 12.1MP Digital Camera with 20x Optical Image Stabilized Zoom with 3-Inch LCD (Black) (OLD MODEL)

text_fidelity_a:
Bose CineMate 1 SR Home Theater Speaker System (Black) I bought this system to replace my Yamaha YSP-500 and a fairly sizeable subwoofer. My issue was that we were doing a remodel of our living room to put in a wall with a fireplace and stonework where our existing entertainment center was. Because the Yamaha projector is fairly substantial, mounting it directly to the wall wasn't an option, so I would have had to build another shelf or do something else. I would have also had to relocate the sub which would have meant either buying some sort of wireless set up or running a cable under the floor and into the wall.

Since the Bose speaker is much slimmer and lighter, has an available wall bracket, and the sub is wireless I thought I had the solution to my problem. For that part, the Bose is great. It was easy to mount, is relatively unobtrusive, and having more flexibility with the placement of the sub is really nice. If you have space limitations or just don't want to mess with running speaker wire (or can't) then this is a good alternative.

This is also a good alternative for people that just want to plug something in and have it work. If you are technically challenged, or just don't want to invest the time in setting up a home theater then this is a usable solution. Most people could have this up and running (including configuration) in less than 20 minutes.

I thought the sound quality is pretty decent. I don't know that it is significantly better than the older (and cheaper) Yamaha Sound Projector that it replaced. Unlike some reviewers, I thought voices (at least on television shows) were clearer and easier to hear than what I was used to. The bass was crisp, but I haven't experienced the punch I am used to with my Yamaha sub. Granted the Bose Accoustimass module is a lot smaller, but there is a very noticeable difference.

There are two areas that I took a star away for each. One is obviously cost. At around $1000, I would say that this would be a better value. At its current price I think that you are not really getting what you pay for. For all the trade-offs, I think there are cheaper alternatives.

The second is the fact that it lacks any sort of display or ability to customize. You can't make any sort of sound profiles (movies, sports, etc), you don't have anything like a night mode, and there is no display whatsoever to indicate something as simple as volume level. Some people may like that, but to me it was rather annoying. For the price, I think you should be able to do a little more with it. Again, if you are the plug-and-play type, this probably won't bother you.

Overall, other than the size and wireless sub, this is not an improvement from my Yamaha Sound Projector. I think it's good, but if I had to do it over again I would probably look at other, cheaper options.
text_fidelity_b: Bose CineMate 1 SR Home Theater Speaker System (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Monster ScreenClean Soft Touch Wipes, Screen Cleaner Wipes for Computer Screens, TV, Phones, Tablets, and Car Touch Screens, Home Office, 70 Count After 40-some years on the technical side of electrochemical fabrication (12" wafer fab) and manufacturing that included the IBM PS1 & PS2 birth … cleanliness is Godliness. I've likely tried every chemical variant of cleaner ever invented, though many fewer are now permitted for USA use.

Though impractical for the laptop, some excellent cleaners in the $1000/gal category might be suggested for cleansing strategic missile-related monitors and surfaces. The value and reliability of what device you are cleaning is the most critical consideration when choosing a cleaner. A wrong choice might pay back immediately with bad results, dissolving the anti-reflective coating or lamination of the touch screen overlay, removing specialized keyboard paints, ruining distinctive finishes, etc. For another, that same choice might do a bang-up job on the big screen at home, but when used on a laptop, it slowly dissolves and/or corrodes critical interconnects as you pass through dewpoints on that 17-hour airplane ride to Sydney.

Q: What is the best cleaner to shine on my $1500 laptop?

A: Not the cheapest $4/qt cleaner. Not one of grandma's window elixirs.

Behind the scenes, there is likely no other technical discussion as critical as cleaning and cleaners. Billions are spent every year on the problem. What I know from experience is that an alcohol solvent-based cleaner does a pretty good job erasing the symbology that makes my lighted keyboard legible. I look for a cleaner to remove the latent crusty-goo residue left by that anti-viral covid computer cleaner six months ago. Some cleaners with notionally benign saponifiers that sell under the enviro-friendly, "Green!", "non-GMO!" moniker is known to corrode solder joints and electro-plating to short the keyboard and LCD/OLED out.

Finding the right balance between solvent and saponifiers has not evolved smoothly. Saponifiers remove organics. The stuff that sprays out of your mouth and nose when yelling at the laptop. Solvents remove inorganics like hand cream, french fry grease, and Cheeto dust. I've rolled up all of this wisdom in my 'Rule #446 - Do not buy the cheapest electronics cleaner. Ever.'

This Monster cleaner is not cheap. It's a premium cleaner under a known premium brand. Given Monster brands, cleaning processes are the #1 priority for their established long-lived high-fidelity interconnection. My laptop has a touch screen that demands a non-delaminating cleaner and a lighted keyboard with that funky paint and laser-etched symbology. This Monster cleaner did an unexpectedly quick, no-smudge job on the laptop. All is good.
text_fidelity_b: Monster ScreenClean Soft Touch Wipes, Screen Cleaner Wipes for Computer Screens, TV, Phones, Tablets, and Car Touch Screens, Home Office, 70 Count

text_fidelity_a:
Motorola T200TP Talkabout Radio, 3 Pack GMRS walkie-talkies like this have been around for decades. Unfortunately, the technology hasn't really improved in all that time. The specs that are listed in the description are greatly exaggerated. We only get 4-5 hours of moderate use from the rechargeable batteries. Fortunately, you can replace them with fresh AA batteries in the field to extend your usage time. The 20 mile range is really a hoax. Even the most optimal situation when one of us is on top of a hill and the others are visible in the valley below, we've never gotten more than 10 miles. In clear flat situations like across a lake or a farm field, range is a 3-4 miles at best. In a forest or city where there are lots of obstructions, range can be less than 1 mile.

20 years ago, few people had cell phones so these radios were really popular. Not so much anymore. That means you get much less interference on each channel. We find the radios useful for family outings since the kids don't have cell phones and many of the parks we visit have terrible cell phone coverage.

The radios are fairly lightweight (about 6 ounces each including the batteries). The package includes 3 battery packs and 2 chargers. One of the chargers has a splitter so it can charge 2 radios at the same time. You can also use your micro-USB cell phone charger to charge the radios. You can also use your own rechargeable AA batteries with your own charger. Replacing the batteries is kind of a hassle since the belt clip blocks the battery cover, though I suppose that also helps keep the battery cover in place. No carrying cases or storage case is included, through the radios are pretty durable and the shipping box works well for storage.

Note that USA use requires a Federal FCC radio license. The photo here is from the instruction manual. Many (perhaps most) users violate Federal law and use them without license, but who knows what enforcement will be like in the future. Other countries have stricter laws and I have heard about some tourists getting into trouble using radios like this.
text_fidelity_b: Motorola T200TP Talkabout Radio, 3 Pack

text_fidelity_a:
Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors) This jumpdrive is USB 3.0 (fast) but backward compatible with 2.0. It's a little cheesy looking because of its plastic "bubblegum" look, but the color-coding of the different size drives could be useful. I got the bright green 32 GB USB 3.0 stick for review, and when I put it into my USB port it showed installation files on the drive for both Windows and Mac. I double-clicked the Mac for my MacBook Pro, and it presented me with the installation screens. It was a little confusing how to get the software installed, and initially I had to install it on my computer to access the installation for just the flash drive; it's supposed to be optional to install it on your computer, but it wasn't apparent how to bypass computer installation. I had to delete my computer vault after it was created to get it off my computer.

Another confusion is that you are taken to a website with an offer for an Encryptstick software upgrade for a reduced cost or free for a 14-day trial. Apparently, all the best features of this device are not available if you just use the stick as a USB drive with the standard "Encryptstick Lite" app that comes with it. You will have AES encryption, but not the "military grade encryption," whatever that means. (The website lists the option to encrypt vaults with 128, 256, or 512-bit AES ciphers [1024-bit coming], registered and government approved, FIPS 140-2 compliant). Here are the other features listed on the website and, again, it's not clear which come with the standard installation and which with the upgraded one:

Runs on Multiple OS computers and all recently made USB flash drives
Encrypt & Decrypt Your Private Files
Easy to Use Encryption Interface [debatable!]
Speedy Auto-Updater
Lost Flash Drive Data Recovery Feature
Advanced Virtual Keyboard
Lock out Computer Installation is Optional - Not Essential
Lock out No Admin Rights Required
File Wipe Instant Lock
Quick Search, Live Search
Automatic Timeout
Limited Login Attempts
File Wipe File Shredder

I went on and purchased the upgrade (12.99 to Lexar users instead of the usual 39.99) because the advanced backup features are only available with the upgraded version and I did want them, but I thought it was a little sneaky how they presented all this. It's really not clear that you don't have to get the upgrade to make the stick itself work. Once you've purchased the upgrade, you are given links to download the upgrade for all versions (PC, Mac, and Linux) in an email.

Somehow I wound up with both the EncryptStick Lite and EncryptStick apps both running at the same time. I could not close out of either one of them, and attempting to eject the jumpdrive gave me an error saying I needed to close out of both apps. I had to force-quit the Lite app. That made me nervous about the whole thing.

I have to mention the following experience because, for me, it was an issue. The little lanyard (about the length of the drive when installed) is not attached when you take it out of the package, and I had a heck of a time getting it threaded through the end. The cord won't bend through the jumpdrive's hole, so it requires using an implement of some come to grasp the thread end and pull it through. My tweezers were too large, and so was the end of the large paperclip (all I had), so I wound up having to strip off the coating on an old bobby pin that I just happened to have lying in a drawer. Even then, I had to pop up part of the plastic cover on the front of the drive case a little to work the thread through, and I was worried about destroying the drive in the process. This whole process was very aggravating, so I think it would be better if they sold these with the lanyard already attached. Customers can then remove it if they don't want it, but I think the lanyard is quite useful. If you have more than one of these drives, you could hang them all up on a keyholder at your desk, then pull one off to take with you as needed.

Please note that I am downrating this product because of the initial confusion and hassles above, although in fairness this is not a good indication of the reliability and performance of the jumpdrive once the software and lanyard are installed. Consider this review to be of the initial experience with the jumpdrive and software. If I discover any more problems as I use this drive over time, I will come back and post them. For now, though, I'm tired of fooling with it!
text_fidelity_b: Lexar JumpDrive S35 64GB USB 3.0 Flash Drive - LJDS35-64GABNL (Assorted colors)

text_fidelity_a:
ASUS C201PA-DS02 11.6-Inch Laptop (Navy Blue) This is my first time using a Chromebook and I didn't know what to expect. I mean it's sort of like a laptop in size but it runs on Chrome, not Windows.

Start-up was fast, almost super fast. You open the cover and BAM, within seconds, you're online. Very cool.

The display is HD and very crisp. I viewed a couple of Netflix nature movies and the display was stunning. No lag or fuzziness. There's a Micro HDMI so you can view on a big screen, but a cable is not included.

The wi-fi is dual-band 802.11 and is fast as well. I had no issues connecting at home, work, or the local coffee shop.

There is 16gb of local storage, but Google includes 100gb of Google Drive storage for 2 years. Personally I've never used more than 3gb of storage, so 100gb should be adequate for most people.

The internal speakers weren't great, but they didn't suck either. Sound was crisp but slightly muted. A pair of USB speakers took care of this. Soon I was rocking in the coffee shop (i forgot my headphones).

Because of my big fingers I'm not a fan of the pad thingy. I was able to plug in a bluetooth mouse and was up and running within 30 seconds. At first I wasn't sure if the Chromebook would allow peripherals, but it did with no issues.

The battery is stated to last 13 hours. I haven't gone that far yet, but I've gotten a solid 5 hours of mixed internet/video streaming use and still had 50% battery left.

The fit and finish is top notch although the top cover can be a finger print magnet. I just throw a microfiber cloth in my bag.

The keyboard has ample sized 'chicklet' keys which are soft and silent. My big fingers had no issues hitting other keys by accident.

In closing, I'm a convert!

My laptops were mainly used for the internet and watching movies. With everything online, like Netflix, Hulu, and Prime movies, this Chromebook rocks!
text_fidelity_b: ASUS C201PA-DS02 11.6-Inch Laptop (Navy Blue)

text_fidelity_a:
Sony Xperia Ear Duo True Wireless headset – Black EDIT: Sony sent me a replacement unit under warranty because of the broken charger. The new unit works as advertised, so I'm upgrading my review to 3 stars. Some users may rate this more highly because of your needs. I give it 3 stars because they are difficult to use, uncomfortable to wear, have mediocre battery life, and are very expensive.

I wanted to give these a fair and thorough test, but unfortunately quality seems to be lacking and it died after just 2 days. First, the rubber ear tip on the right side kept falling off every time I took the earpiece out. Maybe I'm clumsy or maybe it is too fragile, but either way this is really annoying. Second, the battery life is terrible. The battery life indicator dropped from 70% to 30% after just 20 minutes of listening to music. Finally, the charger died. One of the little pins that connected the charger device to the earpiece broke off (or never was attached). Without it, I cannot recharge the right earpiece and since this is a non-standard charger, the whole thing is now useless.

Even if the headphones were 100% functional, here are some general thoughts:
1. Sound quality is very good for headphones that allow you to hear your surroundings. I don't have to take the headphones off to talk to someone standing next to me.
2. That is great because getting these things on or off is much more cumbersome than any other headphone I have ever tried.
3. The user manual really wants you to control these things using finger and head gestures. Maybe my memory is poor, but I can never remember all those things. Even when I'm reading the manual and trying to use the gestures, half the time they don't work.
4. This headset is expensive if all you can do is listen to music and phone calls. They are heavily advertising the "personal assistant" feature as well. The personal assistant feature asks for all kinds of permissions so it can read your messages and emails to you. After the recent Facebook hack, I am really reluctant to grant all these permissions.
5. The personal assistant works best if you have the headphones on all the time instead of just occasionally when you listen to music. However, the advertised battery life of these headphones is only 2-4 hours and my experience is less than that. Constantly recharging these things is a real hassle. Even taking them on and off several times a day is a real hassle.
6. The headphones are cumbersome to take on and off and wear and they are cumbersome entirely because they want to remove the wire between the 2 sides that cheaper headsets have. I don't think that tradeoff is worthwhile if you're not wearing these constantly and you can't wear them constantly because of the battery life.
text_fidelity_b: Sony Xperia Ear Duo True Wireless headset – Black

Lepow Portable Monitor - 2023 C2 15.6 inch FHD 1080P Portable Display with IPS Screen, Foldable Kickstand, Dual Speakers, Type-C HDMI Mini DP Port for Laptop PC Phone Xbox Switch PS5, Iron Gray First off I was a little irate with this product. I was so excited when it arrived today, that I was tracking Amazon. Okay upon opening this monitor the packaging was done right. Everything you need is in the box.

I am a coder and I needed this monitor to work perfectly with my Macbook Pro 2020 version.
This is from my experience others may have not experiences the trails and frustration I dealt with. I was seriously debating on returning it to the UPS store.
I couldn't get the picture to work. I worked on it for about 30 minutes and started surfing the web. I came across a video and watched this guy plug it in on the left side and it worked. So it will help to read and look at the pictures in the booklet first.

To save you the hours of frustration I experienced with this product, I will give you the information you need for this to work minutes out of the box. If you want to read this instead of the book.

1. Plug the USB-C port into the left side of the monitor. (I did all the other ports except that one.)

2. Plug into your USB-C port and the picture will work. No stand by or black-outs unless you use all the other ports besides the one on the left.

3. Issue: How do you have more than one thing on the screen?
System preferences>display>arrangement (important!)
The white box in the arrangement tab above the box, that is your Macbook. The second box is your monitor. If you want the monitor on the right side, move the box without the white bar over to the right. The same goes for the left. Now drag that picture over to the side your monitor is on and Bam!!! Beauty!

4. Problem: You don't want to use the volume on the monitor you'd rather listen on your Macbook.
System preferences>sound>output>slide that over to MacBook Pro speakers and take it off that Z1 crap. (That took me a while too.)
Overall, after the stress and migraine, I endured trying to figure this product out. I will have to say it works perfectly for my needs for now.
You better bet your bottom dollar if I have one issue with this product I will be returning it ASAP! Spending more than a hundred dollars on any product during COVID 19 is too much.

Overall I am glad I made this purchase and I'm glad I didn't take it to the UPS store to return it.
text_fidelity_b: Lepow Portable Monitor - 2023 C2 15.6 inch FHD 1080P Portable Display with IPS Screen, Foldable Kickstand, Dual Speakers, Type-C HDMI Mini DP Port for Laptop PC Phone Xbox Switch PS5, Iron Gray

text_fidelity_a:
Fire TV Stick with Voice Remote This product has a lot of promise, but fails to deliver in some areas, and is just plan not user friendly in others.
My experience on this product was that it arrived a day late, and when it arrived it would not work with my Visio High Definition Television. The TV either did not recognize it or it did not recognize my TV. So I dragged another High Definition Television into the room that I had (LG) and it immediately began working. Set up was fairly simple, however some of the setup features are where my annoyance began. This device every now and again asks for codes for WiFi and other settings that were already input. Things like Hulu and Netflix ask me every now and again if I want to sign up or login as an existing user. Why does it randomly do this? My Roku remembered me, why cant this. Amazon Prime offers password protection to prevent family members or other unwanted individuals from charging content to your credit card through a six digit pin. However the only way to input that pin (other than downloading an app to your phone) is to use an awkward scroll wheel, and additionally oddly marked buttons to get through the numerous number menu options. It is a bit of a pain. The voice control feature is a waste of money, it only finds items that Amazon can charge you for. I attempted to look up Thomas the Train for my daughter which was not only available free for Prime Members but was also on Netflix and Hulu which I had and was free, instead all it would find was items that Amazon could charge for. This is a common problem with the voice command feature. This when coupled with the horrendous navigation menus and difficulty finding what you want make this a poor choice considering other options from Roku, Apple TV and others. A little more tweaking and this could be a great product.
text_fidelity_b: Fire TV Stick with Voice Remote

text_fidelity_a: Samsung Galaxy Note 10.1 2014 Edition (32GB, White) I bought tablet  a few days after release. It has super hardware specs and a beautiful screen; however, it seemed to me Samsung rushed its release in order to beat several other tablet coming to market. This Spen is great, yet the Note program needs to be refined to include a few more enhancement similar to the IOS program Notability. There are several bugs that Samsung should have addressed prior to release, and I am sure they will fix with future updates. The bezel appears to be cheap plastic, but I did like the leather back cover. The Polaris Office program is very good but lacks documentation. I returned both of the Notes I tried. One came slightly damaged and both had several software related issues. This does not mean this is a bad product but it is far from polished. I love Samsung and have owned several of their products including a two Samsung Galaxy phones and a Samsung Galaxy 5.0 Player. Their are several positives here, but as it stands now,  this is not a iPad replacement. It is not nearly polished enough and its battery life is not nearly as strong. For $600.00, it should be a lot more refined. I buy the best product from whoever makes it, and I have zero allegiance to any brand. My agenda is about work and productivity, and this product gets it done with several fixable bumps in the road.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung Galaxy Note 10.1 2014 Edition (32GB, White)

The USB ports are dated and are not worth it unless you want to charge small devices and only one, maybe two at a time.
This "Surge Protector" has an FCC emblem imprinted on the back, which may be illegal, not sure, but does not actually have the required holographic sticker to prove that it's safe or certified. I'm not sure it's either one.
"If" I were to use this, I would only use this for low wattage electric items that are inexpensive to replace and would not consider it a "Surge Protector" at all. I would also always unplug it when I was finished using it and not leave it plugged in.
All of my surge protectors have the FCC stickers and most also have information on the cord itself. This one has all the specs you see in the listing and says it's a surge protector on the back.
This would be a great deal if it had certification and came with a good warranty, but it doesn't. If you're a gambler and like to take chances, buy it. If not, look for a real surge protector that has protection to back it, and your devices if it fails. Not to mention, this thing might burn your house down one day. I don't think I will be using it for much, if at all, and I would not recommend It, as it is just too risky. 3 stars ✨

Polk Audio ES35 Sound Wall Mount Speakers, Black & Polk Audio ES15 Wall Mount Bookshelf Speaker, Black I'm very pleased with all aspects of this center speaker. The sound quality is excellent. This replaces an old KEF center speaker and the difference can be clearly heard. The Polk has a crisp, clean sound that clarifies and enhances dialog but not at the expense of a nice solid bass (although I also have a subwoofer in the setup).

Aesthetically it's a simple, clean design. Normally I don't pay much attention to the look of a speaker but in this case, since it's a center speaker, it's in my line of sight all the time. It's about as unobtrusive you can get with a center speaker without compromising sound quality and performance. Polk did an excellent job with the design.

I looked at the new version of this (the ES35) and, while there are some small incremental improvements, I didn't consider them to be worth the extra $100 it costs. Plus, this was on a price dip for the differential between the two was $150, making this the clear choice.

While I have been partial to KEF in the past for speakers, the performance of this Polk has really wow'd me. At present I'm using this center speaker with KEF left and right front speakers, and KEF for surround. I've been so impressed with the ES35 that I'll be changing to Polk for my L/R soon, and keep the KEF only for surround (5.1.2 setup).

An excellent center speaker that hits the mark on all counts. Five stars.

text_fidelity_a:
Jaybird Freedom Sprint Bluetooth Headphones - Retail Packaging - Midnight Black Overall I'm very pleased with these ear buds. They are my first pair of bluetooth buds and it has been wonderful to not have to deal with cords, especially when working out. I can't tell you how many times I've hit an earbud cord while exercising and ripped the ear bud from my ear. A real pain in the neck (and ear!).

>>>Pros:

Comfort - These fit very well in my ear. There are different tip sizes to create a good fit and, after trying them all out, I went with the medium size. Very comfortable to wear even for long periods of time.

Stay put - I've yet to have them fall out even when doing aerobic exercises or while on the treadmill.

Sound - they sound pretty good. The sound is not as good as my favorite (and inexpensive) corded buds ([[ASIN:B0053R0WWG RHA MA-350 Aluminium Noise Isolating In-Ear Earphones]]) but they are a solid B+ performer with regard to bass response and overall clarity. Keep in mind that good bass response is affected by how the buds fit in your ear, so it's important to try out different tip sizes to see how they affect sound quality. They do get harsh at loud volumes, but for normal listening they are more than fine for my non-audiophile ears. They do reasonably well at blocking out ambient noise.

Setup - I found it straightforward even though I've never had any experience with setting up bluetooth earbuds.

Size - nice and compact so you don't get the "radar dish" look that larger units can have.

Durability - they have a "sweat proof" guarantee which is nice (although I imagine, like most guarantees, there are some loopholes). Overall build quality is good, with a very solid feel to all components.

>>>Cons:

Battery life - The manufacturer claims a battery life of 4.5 hours but I've yet to get more than 3 hours off a single charge. Plus there's no warning about battery life (until you're almost fully discharged) or a visual indicator of how much charge there is left.

Usability - the buttons on the buds are too small, making it difficult for me to push the right one. A lot of fumbling and mis-presses, making it often easier to deal with volume changes on the device, which kills some of the value of having wireless buds. I guess I lack the nimble fingers of the primary target market.

But overall, I'm pleased. The pros outweigh the cons, and I think this is a solid 4-star device.
text_fidelity_b: Jaybird Freedom Sprint Bluetooth Headphones - Retail Packaging - Midnight Black

Sabrent Wi-Fi Range Extender 300mbps 2.4GHZ 801.11N Multifunction Mini Router / Repeater / Access Point / Client / Bridge - Wall Plug Version (WR-WN300) This is a very effective solution to the problem of WiFi dead zones in my house. While signal strength from my Linksys router is good in most rooms, there’s a few areas (such as the basement) where the signal is so weak that maintaining a connection fast enough to stream movies is problematic (spend lots of time looking at the “buffering” message from Netflix). Using this as a repeater has solved that problem.

It’s very compact – the whole router plugs right into the wall and is about the same size as a typical USB charger or similar device. The indicator lights for network connectivity and data transfer are on the front, but are dim enough that they don’t cause a problem at night.

The only notable negative is that the instructions are spotty at best. Getting this up and running is not a problem if you have experience in router setup, but could be tough if you’ve never done it before.

Although I'm using this only as a repeater, it offers additional functionality. It can be used in router mode so it functions as a router, or WISP mode, where it rebroadcasts a wireless network under a different name. I can't speak to how it works in modes other than repeater, but given it's excellent repeater functionality, I would imagine other modes work just as well.

With the exception of the instructions, zero problems with this. It’s a very effective (and compact) solution to extending WiFi coverage. Highly recommend.

text_fidelity_a:
JVC HARX700 Precision Sound Full Size Headphones - Black I own the HARX900 (2 pairs) and got these as laptop headphones. I connect these to a USB DAC and can really get good sound with the laptop's EQ and the DAC pushing the voltage. These aren't too heavy for my head, have a comfy band and, most important of all, they don't mess with my glasses or press my ears into the glasses. Fully closed headphones tend to be too tight around the ears for glasses and open types have too much sound bleed and environmental intrusion so this semi-closed design is wonderful for me. The 50mm drivers pump tons of good sound and, if you have the right hardware, these sound excellent even at lower volumes. The sound is very balanced and isn't super bass heavy. These are good for jazz, rock, spoken word, and just about anything else. I enjoy the longer cord because I can run this into a mic jack behind a desktop PC and still have plenty of slack. At 48ohms, these take a little more to push than the regular 32ohm cans, but most cell phones will still sound great with these.

The only bad thing is that the pleather ear pads WILL degrade after a couple of years of constant usage and there aren't really any easy ways to replace them. You buy at your own risk in the aftermarket world, but if you can locate a good source of earpads, these are worth keeping for the long haul once you've burned them in. They sound just as good for most applications as the HARX900 and you will want to get a pair for home and for the office.
text_fidelity_b: JVC HARX700 Precision Sound Full Size Headphones - Black

text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell (1st Gen) – 720p HD video, motion activated alerts, easy installation – Satin Nickel I'm an early adopter of lots of "smart everything" internet connected products (Nest stuff, Smart Grill, SmartVents, internet connected cars, etc.). I have found the Ring doorbell to be one of the most useful and reliable of these types of products. Remote functions that are really valuable to me:
* Remotely "greet" and reschedule the delivery guy who was 2 hours late, while you are out doing other other errands. Warning - it does really freak out most delivery guys to hear your voice emanating from the doorbell button !
* Receive confirmation that your tween/teen has made it home from school, even when they don't see fit to call or text. Plus do a body count to see if any "extras" are visiting. Plus also have a concrete, time-stamped log of any late night returns, so you don't have to stay up late to intercept returning teens.
* Capture video evidence of stolen packages, unwanted solicitations, and prowlers.
The cloud recording cost of 30$/yr is a far better value than other services like Next or Flir. Ring is the clear choice for door monitoring as well as a really cool doorbell.

My only caveats for buyers:
* Take care with the physical installation on very rough surfaces like rough stucco. Holes need to exactly align (no slotted mounting holes) plus the mount plate is sensitive to bending. If the most bends too much to conform to the wall, the actual button/bell unit will not attach.
* Make sure your WiFi signal is strong enough in the location where you are planning install the ring. Plaster and stucco (with embedded screening) attenuate WiFi signals. WiFi basestation with beam-forming really do help (one of my neighbors needed to swap an Apple Airport Express for an Airport Extreme Basestation to achieve reliable and no-laggy video, but now the Ring works like a charm)
* Make sure your transformer is putting out an in-spec voltage, for a wired installation. Mine worked fine, but the another neighbor who recommended the Ring to me wen through two units (replaced by Ring), before they determined the doorbell voltage from the transformer was too high. Things worked flawlessly with the third unit when my neighbor moved to unwired operation.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell (1st Gen) – 720p HD video, motion activated alerts, easy installation – Satin Nickel

text_fidelity_a:
Sena 20S-01D Motorcycle Bluetooth 4.1 Communication System with HD Audio and Advanced Noise Control (Dual) This thing is loaded with features,
It will take me awhile to remember all the functions (push this 1,2, or 3 times, or in combo), but typically you only use a personal few, so it gets better.
I have smartphone Bluetooth cell as both phone and music source - and that works well, though the sound for music isn't awesome (though I haven't others to compare to, I just know what great sounds like at the gym, and these sound tinny or music) - but I bought these as communicators first and music second.
You need to read the instructions over and over again, and the handy cards need to be kept with you on the bike ( there is no way you'll remember everything this thing can do).
The ambient mic feature is an interesting bonus.... Not only do they use that to adjust volume and sensitivity , you can activate it to hear into earphones which is handy when I pull up to customs or drive thought and need to hear what's being said.
FM radio works awesome.
The mic that comestibles your mouth allows you to start talking to your babe or bud and fades the music right away, but it isn't perfect as the music doesn't fade back in as well as I'd want (it thinks ambient noise after you both stop talking might still be voices so it kinda cuts in as chunks), so I prefer to just hit the button to initiate discussions and then hit it again when we're done (though that an be annoying too if there's a string of short discussions).
The other thing is it is supposed to allow you to give voice commands for most key tasks while riding (instead of reaching and finding buttons)... So your driving along and listening to tunes (or not), and say "hello Sena"... That activates the command prompts to speed dial somebody, turn on/off music or radio, or go to next song, or lots of stuff.... It works great in your living room but rarely ever while riding, and I've played with all the levels or think I have. I wish you could use whistling into the mic as a triggering option.... Good news is you quickly learn where the button is for forcing voice prompting so you don't have to keep talking to yourself forever...
There's also this double tap feature that is supposed kick in voice prompting when you tap the unit twice... Great idea, but despite many taps, many places, and not just softly, I only managed to get that to kick once in a month of efforts of the bike.
And yes practice all this in your living room because you don't want to be distracted on the bike. I did the livingroom thing and still took a lot of short rides to realize there's a lot to learn.
Despite what may seem like gloom above, this is one powerful, feature packed unit which has a lot of things I wanted, but I need to get better at, or for firmware updates to continually improve (which they have been).
text_fidelity_b: Sena 20S-01D Motorcycle Bluetooth 4.1 Communication System with HD Audio and Advanced Noise Control (Dual)

text_fidelity_a:
Linksys WiFi Extender, WiFi 6 Range Booster, Dual-Band Booster, Internet Repeater, 2,000 Sq. ft Coverage, Speeds up to (AX1800) 1.8Gbps - RE7310 You should know up front that this extender only works wirelessly with dual-band WiFi routers (routers with both 2.4GHz and 5GHz).

But it will work as a hard-wired range extender for single-band routers (2.4GHz) using an ethernet cable.

If you have a single band router like we do, it will not detect the wireless network or connect wirelessly. If our neighborhood is any indication, this extender won't work with most home routers. Out of the ten or so visible wireless networks in our area, the extender only detected one or two. The two it detected were two of the weaker signals, but I assume were dual band signals the extender would work with.

After several frustrating attempts to get it connected wirelessly, I spent about an hour with customer support before being informed of this limitation on the extender. The product listing says "compatible with all Wi-Fi routers," and it may be compatible with all routers if set up as a wired extender, but apparently it isn't compatible with all as a wirelessly connected extender. If you want wireless connection to your router, check your router's capability and make sure it is a dual-band router before ordering.

As I mentioned, I did get it set up as a wire-connected extender using an ethernet cable. And it works well for that. It puts a good strong WiFi signal all over our house and much of the yard. I'm giving it four stars for that.
text_fidelity_b: Linksys WiFi Extender, WiFi 6 Range Booster, Dual-Band Booster, Internet Repeater, 2,000 Sq. ft Coverage, Speeds up to (AX1800) 1.8Gbps - RE7310

text_fidelity_a:
LotFancy Laptop Cooler Cooling Pad with 5 Quiet Fans for 12-17" Notebook, Dual USB Ports Disclaimer: I was sent this product to evaluate so that I could write an informed review.

Actually this is my second LotFancy cooling pad, and I took it because I do like their products. I haven't had any bad experiences with them except for breaking off one of the little plastic stops that keeps your laptop from sliding off the pad when the rear is elevated, but that was entirely my fault. I left the pad on the floor and someone stepped on it. Can't blame LotFancy for that.

The design of this pad is kind of interesting. It has two controls, one for the large center fan and the other for the four smaller side fans. This, plus the width of the pad itself, allows you to use various sizes of laptop efficiently. If you have a small one, you never need to turn on the side fans. If you have a 17" one, they're in position to help you cool it. I'm curious as to why the green light (signaling that the center fan is on) is set so much lower than the light for the side banks. A strange feature, though not something I have a problem with. It's just odd.

The pad is adjustable to seven different heights (including flat), so you've got a lot of positions to choose from. I write in a variety of places around the house, so this is one of my favorite things about the pad. It allows me to work without having to find all sorts of things to prop my laptop on. The locking mechanism is solid. Since it's USB-powered, there's an extra USB port at the back so that you don't lose that functionality. Most cooling pads have some way of doing this, so it's expected rather than special. It's quiet, but it's far from super silent.

It's a good pad. Yes, some of the construction seems a bit flimsy, but my other LotFancy pad has held together just fine and I see no reason to think this one won't.
text_fidelity_b: LotFancy Laptop Cooler Cooling Pad with 5 Quiet Fans for 12-17" Notebook, Dual USB Ports

I have the "typical" rural setup. One device is on the house, wired to my main router, the other is on the barn (300 feet line of sight away), to downlink to attach to my solar electric monitor.

At first, was having issues getting it to assign IP addresses on the barn access point. No matter what I tried, it did not seem to work correctly. Had plenty of signal, but was not assigning addresses correctly.

Contacted customer support, explained the issue (and, pro tip, here) included screenshots of ALL configuration screens. "Jason" replied the next day suggesting that, since I was configured as a , I should set the "Repeater Mode" in the wizard to "Bridge", as opposed to "Gateway", which is opposite of what the UI in the config suggests. Once I did this, all is working as expected, and I have full connectivity now in my barn, just like I had run a wire between them.
text_fidelity_b: WAVLINK AC600 Outdoor Weatherproof Wi-Fi Range Extender-Dual Band 2.4 & 5GHz Long Range Wireless Internet Signal Extender Booster&Router/AP/Repeater/WISP Mode with POE,No WiFi Dead Zones for Home

text_fidelity_a: Lenovo Chromebook C330 2-in-1 Convertible Laptop, 11.6" HD Display, MediaTek MT8173C, 4GB RAM, 64GB Storage, Chrome OS, Blizzard White Chromebook prices range from around $100 to over $1000. Better Chromebooks have Intel Core CPUs for great performance. The much cheaper Mediatek system in this Chromebook gives it mediocre performance, especially for intensive games or for business users who open lots of tabs simultaneously and frequently switch between them. On the plus side this Chromebook has a useful 4GB of RAM, a sharp colorful IPS screen, a touch screen that works great with Android apps, a very responsive (for swiping) touchpad, and reliable WiFi (much better than my HP laptop). On the minus side, the white plastic shell looks and feels a little cheap, the screen is not very bright, and the touchpad's button feels a little clunky. In summary, if you can't afford more than $300, this is a good choice for casual users who only have a few tabs open at once and use it mostly for email, Facebook, web surfing, and streaming music or videos. If you can afford $350 to $400, you will have several choices with more powerful CPUs for more intensive users.

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Paperwhite E-reader (Previous Generation - 2015 release) - White, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi, Ad-Supported I was really skeptical about getting one of the newer kindles since I was a die hard kindle fan when they first came out. I always like my electronics to have buttons and especially my kindle since I tend to read with one thumb on the screen itself I worried that if I upgraded to this, my thumb would either end up turning pages too soon or it wouldn't be sensitive enough to read my thumb when I wanted to. My old kindle no longer took a charge after 6 years so I had to upgrade and literally the only reason I went with this over anything else (I was wanting to get another one of my old kindles) was the backlight. I have insomnia so I'm often awake in bed with my snoring boyfriend next to me so having a light on isn't an option so having a kindle with a backlight would be ideal.

Turns out my worry over not having a button was all in vain! The touch screen has just the right amount of sensitivity. It's not so sensitive that resting my thumb on the screen where it's comfortable activates anything, but it's not so dull that I can't turn the pages easily. The back lighting is adjustable so I don't have to blind myself and I don't have to use it if I don't want to if I've got plenty of natural light. The screen is clear and crisp, it fits comfortably in my hand and the amount of books I can fit on there is insane! I've currently got 200 titles and I've still got plenty of room for more. It moves faster than my old kindle and the charge is amazing. I've been using it for over a month now and I'm still at 25% battery without charging it once aside from the day I received it.

This is by far the best kindle I've ever had!
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Paperwhite E-reader (Previous Generation - 2015 release) - White, 6" High-Resolution Display (300 ppi) with Built-in Light, Wi-Fi, Ad-Supported
